---
title: "From FASTQ to Nextflow"
subtitle: "Reproducible bioinformatics for complete beginners"
description: "Learn Conda, containers, Nextflow DSL2, Singularity and SLURM by building and validating a small paired-end NGS workflow."
---

You can understand modern bioinformatics workflow engineering without already
being a programmer. This book starts with ordinary sequencing files and shell
commands, then develops one small analysis into a reproducible Nextflow
workflow that can run locally or through an HPC scheduler.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Paired FASTQ files"] --> B["Raw FastQC"]
    B --> C["Trim Galore"]
    C --> D["Post-trim FastQC"]
    C --> E["Bowtie2 + SAMtools sort"]
    E --> F["BAM validation"]
```

## What you will build

By the end, you will have followed the reasoning behind:

- a pinned Conda environment;
- a manually validated NGS workflow;
- a strict Bash implementation;
- a Docker/OCI container image;
- Singularity execution on an HPC system;
- a five-process Nextflow DSL2 workflow;
- local and SLURM execution profiles;
- failure tests, caching and output comparisons; and
- a versioned, evidence-backed release.

## Who this book is for

This book is written for biologists who can use a web browser but may not yet
know what a shell, software channel, container image, workflow channel or job
scheduler is. Every new term is introduced before it is relied upon.

::: {.callout-important title="Scientific scope"}
The example uses deterministic synthetic paired-end reads derived from human
GRCh38 chromosome 22. It contains no patient data. It is a teaching and
reproducibility artifact—not a clinical pipeline, a WGBS pipeline or a
production-scale biological analysis.
:::

## How to use the book

Read the chapters in order the first time. Each practical chapter contains:

1. a biological objective;
2. an engineering objective;
3. a mental model;
4. small copyable commands;
5. expected output;
6. a verification checkpoint;
7. common failures and their causes; and
8. a short exercise.
